newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Japan hopeful on ITA, investment, dubious on labour.
newsitem.headline: Japan hopeful on ITA, investment, dubious on labour.

text.p: The World Trade Organisation (WTO) ministerial meeting could see significant agreement in several areas, but linking labour and trade was not one of them, a senior Japanese official said on Sunday.

He told reporters he saw a distinct possibility of an Information Technology Agreement (ITA) emerging from the conference, and of some progress on the issues of national investment and competition policy and government procurement.

But he doubted concrete steps would be taken toward linking labour standards and trade, being pushed hard by the United States. The idea might at best get a reference in the ministers' declaration, he said.

Ministers from the Geneva-based WTO global trade regulatory body meet in Singapore on December 9-13 to confirm their commitment to open up their nations' markets and set the agenda for the WTO into the 21st century.
The official said informal sessions among participants on Sunday showed "there is emerging a wide measure of agreement on many of the issues, the so-called difficult issues."
In each area, however, there were still what he called hardliners, and the challenge for the rest of the week was "how to persuade these handfuls of hardliners on each issue."
In the case of labour there were just two key hardliners, one a large country and another a medium-size economy, he said.

He declined to name them, but the United States has been outspoken in advocating a trade-labour link, against strong opposition from many developing countries. The United States is also a prominent supporter of ITA.
"For one delegation, ITA and labour are the only major concerns, and I think that's sad," he said.
Being too insistent on the labour issue could get in the way of agreement on other matters, the official said. "We do not want to sacrifice other substantive issues for the sake of labour."
Japan is keen to see progress toward a global agreement on eliminating tariffs on products in the $500 billion world information technology market.
"We would like to come up with an agreement and that is possible, that is possible," the official said, though he cautioned that details might be left to sort out later.
"We may not be able to come up with a sort of airtight agreement of ITA at this stage, but what we can call an agreement should come out at this time in Singapore."

He also expressed hope for progress in the area of foreign investment and competition. Japan and Canada, backed by the European Union, are leading a push to start talks in the WTO on global rules for the treatment of foreign investment, but key developing Asian countries have opposed such discussions.
The EU wants an accord to start talks at the WTO on national competition policies. Japan agrees, but argues this should include anti-dumping measures, or special tariffs.
